Renforcer le français, mais à quel prix: Strengthening French, but at what cost to minorities?

S’il est nécessaire aux yeux de plusieur: Although many see it as necessary, some consider Bill 96, with its far-reaching effects, to be discriminatory. In its drive to address the decline of French, the government wants to intervene in many spheres of society. From the use of the notwithstanding clause to anonymous complaints to public services offered only in French, what worries people, particularly immigrants and members of minorities? A mother goes to the office of the Régie de l’assurance maladie du Québec (RAMQ).
Il lui a fallu plus d’une heure pour s’y: It took her more than an hour to get there from Côte-des-Neiges: on public transit, nothing is familiar, everything is in French, and she is lost. She walks into the downtown building to renew her card, because doing it by phone was too stressful. She tries to explain her situation, but her few notions of French aren’t enough: she hasn’t started francization yet, because she has to work to feed her two children. She does speak a little English, but she is told that since she arrived in Quebec a year ago, she can’t be served in any language other than French. It’s the law, explains the civil servant across from her, whose hands are tied; he risks being reported if he speaks English. He could be fined, and his equipment could be seized. So the woman goes home without health insurance.
Cette situation pourrait éventuellement: This situation could eventually occur if Bill 96 is passed as it was tabled on May 13 by the minister responsible for the French language, Simon Jolin-Barrette. The Quebec government says it is thus responding to the long-demanded update of the Charter of the French Language (Bill 101), adopted in 1977. If passed in its current form, the bill will require that government services be provided only in French, except for people who immigrated less than six months ago, Indigenous people and certain anglophones.
À la suite d’une plainte anonyme, l’Offi: Following an anonymous complaint, the Office québécois de la langue française (OQLF) will be able to seize any electronic equipment, without a judicial warrant, to verify that French is the language of use in businesses. Discussed during public hearings held from September 21 to October 7, the bill stems from the government’s desire to build a “rampart” to protect French, “an essential gesture for the survival of [the] Quebec nation,” in the words of Premier François Legault.
« Je comprends le message, mais dans la: “I understand the message, but in real life, it makes no sense,” says Stephan Reichhold of the Table de concertation des organismes au service des personnes réfugiées et immigrantes (TCRI). “It puts access to essential services at risk,” continues the president of the coalition. He wonders how civil servants and receptionists will be able to verify whether a person arrived less than six months ago.
« Il s’agit de six mois à partir de quan: “Six months from when? For asylum seekers, do we count from their arrival or from when they obtain permanent residence?” he asks. During the public hearings, a few groups suggested extending the six-month period to two years.
À plus forte raison, les programmes de f: What’s more, the francization programs of the ministère de l’Immigration, de la Francisation et de l’Intégration also span two years, and wait times to register for a French course average three months. “Often, one parent starts classes while the other works, and the ministry’s allowances aren’t enough to live on,” Reichhold explains. According to him, Quebec is among the places making the greatest effort to encourage newcomers to learn French: courses are free and everyone can receive financial compensation. “Even if Quebec invests a lot, access to francization leaves something to be desired,” he laments.
Certaines populations, comme les demande: Some populations, such as asylum seekers, temporary agricultural workers or other vulnerable people, have little access to it. “What’s positive is that Bill 96 will make learning French a right,” he acknowledges.
Pour M. Reichhold, rendre les services d: For Reichhold, making government services accessible only in French is above all a “restrictive approach that risks creating a lot of exclusion” among non-francophones. “Immigrants and refugees aren’t directly targeted by the law, but they suffer collateral damage from it,” warns the TCRI president. The bill affects many aspects of life, including school, health, work, youth protection, labour law and businesses. For example, English-language CEGEPs will be capped at 17.5% of all available spots in all Quebec institutions.
La priorité sera donnée aux étudiants an: Priority will be given to anglophone students who completed all of their schooling in English. “The remaining spots will be contested by francophones and allophones, and for the latter, access will be difficult and the competition incredible,” explains Richard Bourhis, a researcher specializing in issues of discrimination. He believes this risks driving away many students who want to become bilingual, especially children of immigrants. “The bill is a constraint for those who hoped their children would find work outside Quebec. They uprooted themselves and sacrificed their careers to give their children better chances,” he insists.
Du côté des entreprises, le projet de lo: On the business side, the bill creates another risk of exclusion.
« Je risque de perdre plusieurs clients,: “I risk losing several clients, because my employees will only be able to speak French,” Samira*, an entrepreneur of Maghrebi origin living in Quebec City, tells us. Bourhis agrees: “Faced with the difficulty of finding work because of racism, or because government institutions are inaccessible, many turned to entrepreneurship. And often the clients are immigrants too, so it will be more complicated for them,” he believes.
La population anglophone québécoise a-t-: Does Quebec’s anglophone population feel like the target of this bill? “This text doesn’t make me very proud,” Houston Riffai tells us cynically from his living room. Born in Montréal, he has an anglophone Quebecer mother and a father who arrived from Syria in the 1970s, at the age of 7. Bilingual, Riffai, who studies at Concordia University, says he is deeply affected by the bill.
Pour lui, le projet de loi 96 renforce l: For him, Bill 96 deepens the split between francophones and anglophones, who make up 8% of the population. “Someone who has lived their whole life in Quebec should have the right to express themselves [in their language],” he says heatedly. He feels the law does nothing to improve his sense of belonging and doesn’t make him want to stay here. Since the announcement of Bill 96, nearly 80% of anglophones are “less proud to be Quebecers,” as are 64% of allophones and 56% of francophones, according to a Léger poll for the Quebec Community Group Network (QCGN), published in 2021.
Les résultats montrent aussi que la majo: The results also show that the majority of non-francophones fear that relations between anglophones and francophones will worsen because of the law. David Birnbaum, MNA for D’Arcy-McGee for the Quebec Liberal Party (PLQ), hears this sense of rejection a lot. He is also the official opposition critic for relations with English-speaking Quebecers, and he tells us he receives many messages of concern about the law. “They are seen as adversaries to the influence of French, when they are allies.
Ça me décourage de voir que les anglopho: It discourages me to see that anglophones are constantly being brought back into line,” he explains. He would like anglophones to be more recognized, because they too are “proud Quebecers.”
Le 28 septembre, lors des audiences publ: On September 28, during the public hearings, Minister Simon Jolin-Barrette said that the Quebec nation encompasses all Quebecers, “including English-speaking communities,” a high point that Marlene Jennings, a former MP and president of the Quebec Community Group Network (QCGN), would like to see made concrete, she tells us by phone.
Au centre du débat du projet de loi et d: At the heart of the debate over the bill and the Charter of the French Language: the advance of English against French. According to the 2016 Canadian census, French is declining as a mother tongue: between 2011 and 2016, the percentage of people whose only mother tongue is French fell from 78% to 77%. The crux of the problem is in Montréal, where French is losing ground in public space: 58% use it on the Island of Montréal, compared with 87% in the rest of Quebec. While these figures prompted the government to update the Charter and protect French, they need to be put in perspective, according to Marlene Jennings. In the same census, 94% of Quebecers were able to hold a conversation in French, regardless of their mother tongue.
Le bilinguisme n’a cessé de croître, sel: Bilingualism has continued to grow, according to <l1>a report by the Office québécois de la langue française</l1>: the percentage of bilingual people rose from 28% in 1971 to 45% in 2016.
Face à ces données sur les langues parlé: Faced with this data on the languages spoken in Quebec, as well as the shortcomings of Bill 101, communities are asking whether a “restrictive approach” is necessary and, above all, whether it is necessary to “jeopardize the fundamental rights of Quebecers,” according to Marlene Jennings. For the second time during its term, François Legault’s government intends to use the notwithstanding clause for Bill 96, as it did for the Act respecting the laicity of the State (Bill 21).
Cette clause permettrait dans ce cas d’o: In this case, the clause would allow the government to override the Canadian and Quebec charters of rights and freedoms. “In other words, no legal recourse will be possible for people whose rights have been flouted,” Marlene Jennings sums up. “We are asking the government to justify why promoting French requires suspending fundamental rights,” she says. By email, Simon Jolin-Barrette’s press attaché responded that it is a “legitimate tool” to ensure “the protection of the French language in Quebec for the benefit of the collective rights of the Quebec nation.”

Les populations autochtones sont elles a: Indigenous peoples are also affected by this bill. The Assembly of First Nations Quebec-Labrador argues that the text tramples the rights of First Nations. “The Legault government’s Bill 96 is an all-out attack on the constitutional language rights of the First Nations,” said Ghislain Picard, chief of the Assembly of First Nations Quebec-Labrador, in a news release.
Les entreprises comptant de 25 à 49 empl: Businesses with 25 to 49 employees will have to implement a francization program and be able to prove that French is the language of work. Under Bill 101, only businesses with more than 50 employees were affected.
Chacun pourra porter plainte anonymement: Anyone will be able to file an anonymous complaint with the OQLF about a service provided in another language. An inspection will be carried out and electronic equipment may be seized.
L’accès aux soins de santé en français,: Access to health care in French, English or another language remains to be clarified. Stephan Reichhold says this right is protected by <l1>section 15 of the Act respecting health services and social services</l1>, but other views are also being heard. Marlene Jennings of the QCGN points out that under Bill 96, only anglophones eligible to receive an education in English could be served in English by the government, which includes hospitals and clinics.
Les recruteurs ne pourront plus exiger l: Recruiters will no longer be able to require English as a hiring qualification, unless the employer shows that “the performance of the duties requires such knowledge,” and also that it has “taken all reasonable means to avoid imposing such a requirement.”
